background.definition: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive, degenerative disease of motor neurons, characterized by upper and lower motor neuron signs affecting multiple body segments.

list.listitem: Age 45 to 74 years: 0.8 to 6.4 per 100,000 persons per year.
Lifetime risk is approximately 1/1000.
Incidence may be higher in men and whites.
The mortality rate for ALS is 0.3 to 4.2 per 100,000 in the United States.
A 2021 study found a range of cost per patient in the published literature of 9741 to 114,605 Euros.
ALS is usually idiopathic.
5% to 10% familial; 20% of familial cases and 2% to 4% of sporadic cases associated with mutations in SOD1 B.
Risk is increased with persons occupied by heavy physical work, professional sports, and work with metals, electromagnetic fields, or chemicals.
A Mendelian randomization study found no association between ALS and autoimmune diseases.
A systematic review of 25 observational studies found no evidence linking medication use with ALS.
Patients experience progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons, with chronic and active denervation of affected body segments.
Bulbar and limb muscles are affected; pathology is not restricted to motor neurons and may overlap with frontotemporal dementia.
Suspect ALS in patients with weakness, fasciculations, dysarthria, or dysphagia. C

Diagnosis depends on finding upper motor neuron signs (such as weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs) or lower motor neuron signs (such as weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations) that affect multiple body segments. C
Order EMG/NCS (which may demonstrate lower motor neuron involvement) and MRI (which may be helpful for excluding other disorders that could mimic ALS). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Multifocal conduction block on nerve conduction studies
Lack of upper motor signs; chronic with onset in early life
Degeneration of upper motor neurons only
Idiopathic lower motor neuron syndrome that is self-limited to the distal upper extremities
Degeneration of lower motor neurons only

list.listitem: The diagnosis of ALS requires the presence of lower motor neuron signs (including EMG features in clinically unaffected muscles), upper motor neuron signs, and progression of symptoms and signs.
The diagnosis of ALS also requires the absence of sensory signs, sphincter disturbances, visual disturbances, Alzheimer-type dementia, autonomic dysfunction, and basal ganglion dysfunction.

Approximately 40% of patients present with bulbar symptoms, most commonly dysarthria (26%) or dysphagia (10%). Up to 75% eventually develop these symptoms at some point in their illness. The remaining patients present with symptoms affecting the limbs, typically painless weakness and atrophy.
Lower motor neuron signs include weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations. Upper motor neuron signs include weakness, spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski signs.
Asymmetry is common; either upper or lower motor neuron signs may predominate at presentation.
Symptoms of respiratory insufficiency (dyspnea on exertion, supine dyspnea, disturbed sleep, and morning headache) are associated with a greater than 50% decrease in vital capacity.
The median time from presentation to definitive diagnosis in one series was 8 months, though this is highly variable (0.4-8.9 months).
EMG/NCS allows identification of lower motor neuron involvement in limbs that may not be clinically affected. EMG/NCS is also helpful for excluding mimics, such as multifocal motor neuropathy.
Most other tests are used to exclude other conditions that might mimic ALS or to monitor disease progression.
MRI of the cervical spine is used to exclude structural causes of upper motor neuron findings in the lower extremities or lower motor neuron findings in the upper extremities.
MRI of the lumbosacral spine is used to exclude structural causes of lower motor neuron signs in the lower extremities.
MRI of the brain is used to exclude structural causes of bulbar findings or upper motor neuron findings in the limbs.
Serum CK levels are elevated in approximately 43% of patients with ALS. The test is insensitive, nonspecific, and does not indicate prognosis or severity.
Serial pulmonary function tests are recommended for monitoring pulmonary status in patients with ALS.
Swallowing evaluation is used to identify patients with bulbar symptoms at risk for aspiration.

Suspect ALS in patients with weakness, fasciculations, dysarthria or dysphagia. Physical examination is focused on detection of upper and lower motor neuron signs involving multiple body segments (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral).
Serial examinations are often needed to make a definitive diagnosis; see Differential Diagnosis table for conditions commonly misdiagnosed as ALS.
Order EMG/NCS and MRI of the brain and spine to exclude mimics (such as multifocal motor neuropathy) and detect active and chronic denervation.
Diagnosis should be made and delivered by a physician experienced in treating ALS.
summarizes the key elements of office visit for patients with ALS.
Riluzole (50 mg orally, twice daily) slows disease progression in patients with ALS and should be initiated as soon as possible after diagnosis. A
Noninvasive ventilation improves quality of life and survival in patients with symptomatic hypoventilation. A
Invasive mechanical ventilation, using a tracheostomy can improve survival for several months and improve quality of life, but also has a significant effect on caregivers.B

Riluzole 50 mg twice daily is the only drug therapy shown to increase ventilator-independent survival in patients with ALS. Survival is prolonged by approximately 3 months after 18 months of treatment.

A trial randomized 220 patients to riluzole + placebo versus riluzole + low-dose interleukin-2 injections monthly for 18 months. There was no difference in mortalty (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.22, p = 0.33). A post hoc adjusted analysis found a benefit in the subgroup with low CSF phosphorylated-neurofilament heavy-chain (CSF-pNFH) levels that requires further study.

For patients with the pathogenic variant of SOD1, a randomized trial with 108 participants compared tofersen with placebo. After 148 weeks, early initiation compared with later initiation was associaited with modestly slower declines in clinical and respiratory function, muscle strength, and disease-specific quality of lilfe (ALS Assessment Questionnaire 5 score 17 vs 22.5 points). Survival was also prolonged.

A meta-analysis identified 5 RCTs with 566 participants comparing edaravone with placebo. There were small benefits seen for edaravone in terms of grip strength and the ALSFRS-R score, but no differences in FVC, pinch strength, or the ALS Assessment Questionnaire (ALSAQ-40).

A propensity score matched cohort study compared 194 patients receiving IV edaravone and 130 matched patients receiving standard therapy. No differences in disease progression or other outcomes was observed.

A randomized trial assigned 177 patients in a 2:1 ratio to sodium phenylbutyrate 3 gm + taurursodiol 1 gm once daily for 3 weeks and then twice daily for 24 weeks. Patients in the intervention group slightly smaller decline than the placebo group (-1.24 vs -1.66 points/month, p = 0.03) on the 48 point ALS Functional Rating Scale. The difference was 2.32 points on the 48 point scale at 24 weeks, which is of questionable clinical significance.

Many compounds (eg, reldesemtiv, verdiperstat, testosterone, immunoglobulin, cyclosporine, interferon, antibiotics, vascular endothelial growth factors, and stem cells) were either ineffective in clinical trials or the trials to date have been inconclusive.
A small RCT found no benefit of fecal microbiota transplant in 27 randomized patients with ALS.
An RCT of 80 patients found no benefit to the MAO-B inhibitor rasagiline.
A systematic review identified 3 studies comparing perampanel with placebo and found no evidence that it improves function. Adverse effects include aggression, dysarthria, and sleepiness.

For sialorrhea, guidelines recommend benztropine, transdermal hyoscyamine, atropine, trihexyphenidyl hydrochloride, or amitriptyline. A Cochrane review found 4 small RCTs with 110 participants who had motor neuron disease and intractable sialorrhea. They concluded that the evidence was strongest for botulinum toxin B injections of the salivary glands and oral dextromethorphan with quinidine.
For pseudobulbar affect (emotional lability), guidelines recommend amitriptyline or fluvoxamine.
For patients with acute episodes of dyspnea, lorazepam (0.25-2.5 mg sublingually) can provide temporary relief.
For patients with episodes of dyspnea lasting more than 30 minutes or with chronic dyspnea, morphine (start at 2.5 mg orally or subcutaneously) can provide relief.

Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tubes are indicated for symptomatic dysphagia. Because of the higher risk of complications in patients with respiratory insufficiency (forced vital capacity [FVC] <50%), guidelines recommend the insertion of enteral access before there is significant respiratory compromise. A Cochrane review found no RCTs comparing enteral tube feeding with other options.
The decision to place a feeding tube should depend primarily on symptomatic choking and inadequate calorie intake, not tests of swallowing function.
For patients who decide to use chronic ventilation, tracheostomy tubes are indicated.
A neuroprosthesis with 256 intracortical electrodes successfully restored the ability to communicate using speech.
Vitamin C showed some benefit in a mouse model of familial ALS. Human data are lacking, but many patients with ALS take vitamin C.
Antioxidants, while generally well tolerated, have not been found effective in treating patients with ALS.
Physical therapy, occupational therapy, orthotics, mobility devices, and supportive equipment are recommended for most patients.
Consider supplemental nutrition, communication devices, or speech therapy as needed.
A Cochrane review identified only a single trial of exercise for the treatment of spasticity in patients with ALS, which was inconclusive.

A systematic review with different inclusion criteria identified 7 RCTs with 322 ALS patients. Functional scores and forced vital capacity were significantly improved in the exercise group, while muscle strength and quality of life were not.
Supportive treatment may be helpful for cognitive issues, frontal lobe dysfunction, and emotional dysregulation.
For symptomatic hypoventilation or FVC less than 50% expected, begin discussion about noninvasive ventilation or invasive mechanical ventilation.
There is insufficient evidence to support mechanical insufflation/exsufflation to improve cough/mucus clearance in patients with ALS.

Noninvasive ventilation, including continuous positive airway pressure devices using an oral or nasal delivery mask, is generally a temporary intervention used to increase quality of life, but has no effect on longevity.
Invasive mechanical ventilation, using a tracheostomy can improve survival for several months and improve quality of life, but also has a significant effect on caregivers.
Avoid using oxygen alone because of retention of carbon dioxide and dry mouth.
A small uncontrolled trial suggested a possible benefit to repeated intrathecal administration of autologous mesenchymal stem cells. Further study is needed.
Referral to a neurologist should be initiated as soon as the diagnosis is suspected.

Diagnosis should be delivered by a physician experienced in the diagnosis of ALS, its treatment, and its natural history. Improper delivery of the diagnosis is common and may be harmful. Specific guidelines address how the diagnosis of ALS should be delivered: in person, stepwise, with written materials and the reassurance that the patient would not be abandoned.

Hospitalization is indicated for respiratory distress (unless the patient elects against artificial ventilation) and for the inability to take adequate water or nutrition (unless patient elects not to have artificial nutrition).
Consider hospice care in the terminal stages of illness.
ALS is a progressive disease, though the rate of progression is highly variable. B
Median survival after diagnosis is 1 to 3 years without mechanical ventilation. B
Patients require close follow-up, particularly newly diagnosed patients and patients with significant disability. Serial measurements of respiratory function are recommended. C
Elevated levels of c-reactive protein are associated with a worse prognosis.

A clinical prediction model (http://www.encalssurvivalmodel.org/) had good discrimination and calibration for predicting the outcome of death or need for 23+ hours per day of mechanical ventilation. It had 8 predictors: bulbar versus non-bulbar onset, age at onset, definite versus probable or possible ALS, diagnostic delay, forced vital capacity, progression rate, frontotemporal dementia, and presence of a C9orf72 repeat expansion.

feature.caption: Key Elements of Caring for the Patient with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
feature.feature_body:
Initiate therapy • Early referral to a specialty center
• Consider riluzole early in course
• Consider clinical trials
Monitor pulmonary function (vital capacity, forced vital capacity) • Early noninvasive ventilation
• Early discussion about mechanical ventilation
Nutrition and feeding • Monitor weight, symptoms of dysphagia
• Early use of feeding tube if pulmonary function is declining (before forced vital capacity is <50% of predicted), inability to maintain adequate oral intake, or if losing weight
Quality of life • Dysarthria: consider assistive devices, speech therapy
• Mobility, falls: physical therapy, occupational therapy, orthotics, power wheelchair, home safety devices, home modification to improve access and safety
• Secretions, drooling: symptomatic treatment
• Mood, cognitive symptoms: amitriptyline or fluvoxamine
Data from EFNS task force on management of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: guidelines for diagnosing and clinical care of patients and relatives. An evidence-based review with good practice points (EFNS).
